title: Inference, serving and model operations
summary: One registered version, two contracts: a scored table and an endpoint. Trace a request, hold it to its signature, size its concurrency, release by traffic, and read inference tables and monitors as evidence that keeps drift a hypothesis until delayed labels test it.
outcomes: Choose batch or online scoring for a consumer and trace one request across authorization, routing, signature enforcement, feature lookup and prediction with a timing at each hop.
Predict whether a request body is accepted, converted or refused, and write a local contract test that proves the package's contract without a managed call.

Estimate provisioned concurrency from arrival rate and service time, plan a staged release with an evidence gate per stage and a one-step rollback, and read inference tables and a data profiling monitor as evidence.

Separate drift from verified quality loss under delayed and biased labels, classify an incident by its evidence layer, and fill an operational scorecard and a cost-driver list without provisioning or pricing anything.
startingAssumptions: The MLflow module has given the model a version in Unity Catalog with a signature, an environment and an alias earned by evidence.
The features module has explained point-in-time features and online stores; this module uses them at inference time without re-deriving them.
editorialRationale: Serving teaching fails when it starts from an endpoint's configuration screen, so the module starts from two consumers of one registered version and lets each mechanism, the contract, the capacity estimate, the feature lookup, the traffic split, appear as the consumer's need. Evidence comes before verdicts: the inference table and the monitor are taught as tables to read, drift is held as a hypothesis until delayed and biased labels test it, and an incident is classified by the layer that produced its evidence. Every managed-serving example is a sketch labelled not executed, the contract test is local, and cost is a list of drivers with symbols for rates, so nothing here requires a workspace or invents a price.

A registered version, addressed by name and alias, scores a Spark DataFrame through a pyfunc Spark UDF; AI Functions including ai_query can score from SQL inside pipelines and jobs.

A model logged with the feature engineering client keeps references to its features; in batch, score_batch joins point-in-time correct feature values from the offline store to rows that carry only the keys, then scores them.

claims.description: Inference tables log each request and response into a Unity Catalog Delta table, joinable with labels for evaluation and retraining; an AI Gateway-enabled variant, which Databricks recommends, and a legacy variant are documented with different columns, and rows can take up to an hour to appear.

Data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring) writes a profile metrics table and a drift metrics table per monitor; the InferenceLog profile adds performance metrics when prediction and label columns are present, and drift is computed against a baseline table or consecutive windows.

MLflow schema enforcement validates inputs against the signature before the model runs: missing required inputs raise, undeclared inputs are ignored, columns match by name, and column-based signatures accept only lossless type conversions, such as int to double but not long to double.

For a model logged with the feature engineering client, the endpoint uses the keys in a request to look up precomputed features from a Databricks Online Feature Store, which is powered by Lakebase, or from a third-party online store.

concepts.definition: MLflow's check of request columns and types against the logged signature before the model runs, after the server has parsed the JSON body.

concepts.definition: The number of requests an endpoint can process at once; requests beyond it wait in a queue.
concepts.example: A Small endpoint maps to 4 units as read at search time; 60 requests per second at 80 ms offer 4.8, more than it can hold.

concepts.definition: An endpoint option that lets provisioned concurrency fall to zero after inactivity, at the price of a cold start.

concepts.definition: Precomputed features fetched from an online store by the keys in a request instead of being sent by the caller.

concepts.definition: The percentage of requests routed to each served entity, set and changed in the endpoint configuration.

concepts.definition: Reverting a release by routing all traffic to the previous served entity in one configuration update.

concepts.definition: A Delta table in which the endpoint logs each request, its response, status code, served entity and timing.

concepts.definition: A monitor, formerly Lakehouse Monitoring, that computes profile and drift metric tables over time windows of a table.

concepts.definition: A measured change in the distribution of inputs or predictions between windows or against a baseline; not by itself a quality verdict.

concepts.definition: The true outcome that arrives after the prediction, for some rows only, and only then allows verified quality measurement.

concepts.definition: An operational event classified by the layer that produced its evidence: endpoint health, contract, data and features, or verified quality.

visuals.title: Requests in flight against provisioned concurrency
visuals.alt: Requests in flight against provisioned concurrency. Arrival rate times service time is compared with the four units of a Small endpoint for three traffic patterns.
visuals.caption: Offered load = arrival rate × service time; below the provisioned units nobody waits, above them the backlog grows for as long as the burst lasts. Synthetic teaching example.
visuals.textEquivalent:
The station alone: About 3,000 parts over two shifts is 0.05 requests per second; at 41 ms that offers 0.002 units of work, and a Small endpoint's four units are almost always idle. Table columns: quantity, value. Rows: arrival rate; 0.05 requests/s | service time; 0.041 s | offered load; 0.002 | provisioned units (Small); 4 | capacity; about 97 requests/s | queueing; none. Equation: offered load = 0.05 × 0.041 = 0.002 < 4

Shift-start burst: At shift start the first bins release six requests per second, and a slower 80 ms lookup makes that 0.48; still far under four, so latency stays flat. Table columns: quantity, value. Rows: arrival rate; 6 requests/s | service time; 0.080 s | offered load; 0.48 | provisioned units (Small); 4 | capacity; 50 requests/s | queueing; none. Equation: offered load = 6 × 0.080 = 0.48 < 4

The planner through the endpoint: The planner sends 3,000 parts at 60 per second with 80 ms service: 4.8 units offered to 4. Capacity is 50 per second, so the backlog grows by about 10 requests each second of the 50-second burst, and a station request near its end waits seconds. Table columns: quantity, value. Rows: arrival rate; 60 requests/s | service time; 0.080 s | offered load; 4.8 | provisioned units (Small); 4 | capacity; 50 requests/s | backlog after 50 s; about 500 requests | wait at the end; about 10 s. Equation: offered load = 60 × 0.080 = 4.8 > 4; backlog ≈ (60 − 50) × 50 s ≈ 500

questions.prompt: A Cinderline analyst proposes one path for everything: the station should read the nightly scored table, which is cheaper than an endpoint. What breaks?

options.text: The part on the belt was produced after the nightly job ran, so the table has no row for it.
options.rationale: Batch scores the parts that existed when the job ran; a part produced now has no score until the next run.

options.text: The nightly table cannot hold 3,000 rows.
options.rationale: Row count is not the issue; batch tables scale far past that.

options.text: Delta tables cannot be read by a station application.
options.rationale: Reading a table is possible; the missing row, not the read path, is the problem.

options.text: The endpoint would be deleted automatically when unused.
options.rationale: Nothing deletes an endpoint for being idle; scale to zero only lowers its capacity floor.

questions.prompt: The station app adds a column shift = "A" to every request and changes nothing else. What does the endpoint do?

options.text: It ignores the undeclared column and scores the request as before.
options.rationale: Schema enforcement disregards inputs the signature does not declare; the seven declared columns still match.

options.text: It refuses every request because the column count changed.
options.rationale: Matching is by name, not by count; an extra name is dropped.

options.text: It scores the request but the extra column shifts the feature order and corrupts predictions.
options.rationale: Name-based matching reorders declared columns to the signature's order, so an extra column cannot shift them.

options.text: It creates a new model version that includes the column.
options.rationale: Serving never changes the registered model; the signature is fixed when the version is logged.

questions.prompt: P99 latency on defect-risk rises from 52 ms to several seconds between 23:00 and 23:12 every night; error rate and request bodies are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Another caller sends a nightly burst whose offered load exceeds the provisioned concurrency, so the station's requests wait behind it.
options.rationale: Latency without errors or body changes, on a nightly schedule, is queueing; a batch job routed through the endpoint is the obvious candidate, and the queue-time metric would confirm it.

options.text: The model's quality has degraded.
options.rationale: Quality changes predictions, not latency, and needs labels to be seen.

options.text: The signature was changed on the served version.
options.rationale: A served signature cannot change without a new version, and a contract problem shows as client errors, not latency.

options.text: The inference table stopped logging.
options.rationale: Logging failures lose rows; they do not add latency to responses.

questions.prompt: On release day R+5 the team promotes version 8 to 100% and deletes version 7's served entity to save cost. On R+6 version 8 starts returning 5xx. What has the deletion changed?

options.text: Rollback is now a redeploy of version 7, taking minutes while the station's requests fail, instead of one traffic change.
options.rationale: With the old entity gone there is nothing to route to; a new served entity must be created and built before it can take traffic.

options.text: Nothing; the endpoint keeps version 7's container warm for a week automatically.
options.rationale: No such retention exists; a removed served entity is gone from the configuration.

options.text: Version 8 cannot fail because it is the only entity.
options.rationale: Entity count has no bearing on a container's errors.

options.text: The inference table stops recording version 8's requests.
options.rationale: Logging is unrelated to how many entities exist.

questions.prompt: During the canary you want to compare version 7 and version 8 on the same morning. Which source lets you do that, and what column makes it possible?

options.text: The inference table, because each row records which served entity answered the request.
options.rationale: Only the per-request log carries the entity beside the prediction and inputs, so the two versions can be compared over identical windows.

options.text: Endpoint health metrics, because P99 latency is reported per version.
options.rationale: Health metrics aggregate latency, rate and errors; they do not carry predictions or inputs to compare.

options.text: The model registry, because it stores each version's validation metrics.
options.rationale: Registry metrics come from training-time evaluation, not from the morning's live requests.

options.text: The batch scored table, because it holds both versions' scores.
options.rationale: The batch table scores the planner's rows, not the station's requests, and only with the version the alias named.

questions.prompt: On day 2 of the humid season the monitor shows humidity drift and the flagged rate is 16%. A colleague says: 'The model is degraded; roll back to version 7 and retrain.' What is the correct status of that claim?

options.text: A hypothesis: inputs and predictions moved, which is known, but quality can only be verified when labels arrive for these windows.
options.rationale: Drift is measured; quality loss is inferred, and the inference needs labels. The mitigation while waiting concerns inspection capacity.

options.text: Verified: a flagged rate outside its band is the definition of quality loss.
options.rationale: The band is a trigger for investigation; the rate can rise because defects really rose.

options.text: Refuted: version 7 and version 8 see the same parts, so neither can be worse.
options.rationale: Seeing the same parts does not make either version right; only labels can say.

options.text: Irrelevant: drift is an endpoint-health matter handled by scaling.
options.rationale: Drift concerns data and predictions, not capacity.

questions.prompt: From 06:10 the client-error rate is 100%, P99 latency is unchanged, the monitor shows no drift and version 8 has been at 100% since yesterday. The on-call engineer proposes an immediate rollback to version 7. What is wrong with that first move?

options.text: The evidence is a contract incident: both versions enforce the same signature, so version 7 would refuse the same requests; the first check is the request bodies.
options.rationale: A 4xx spike at flat latency is refused input, not a failing container; rollback changes the entity but not the caller's body.

options.text: Nothing; rollback is always the safest first move.
options.rationale: Rollback answers endpoint-health and release-caused quality incidents; it does not repair a caller's payload.

options.text: The engineer should retrain instead, because a 100% error rate is a quality figure.
options.rationale: An error rate is a status-code measurement; no prediction was made, so there is no quality to judge.

options.text: The engineer should raise the workload size to absorb the errors.
options.rationale: Capacity affects latency and 5xx under load, not client errors at flat latency.

questions.prompt: Finance asks for the monthly cost of the defect-risk endpoint. Which answer is honest today, before anyone has read a pricing page?

options.text: The drivers: about 720 provisioned hours at the Small size, about 90,000 inference-table rows, hourly monitor refreshes and the online store's hours, each priced only once current pricing for the cloud and region is read.
options.rationale: Quantities are known from the design; rates are not, and a number without a dated source is a guess.

options.text: Almost nothing, because the endpoint sits idle most of the time.
options.rationale: Provisioned capacity is held whether or not requests arrive; only scale to zero releases it when idle, and the billing unit is confirmed on the pricing page.

options.text: The same as the batch job, since both use the same model.
options.rationale: The model is shared; the cost drivers are not: hours provisioned versus minutes run.

options.text: A per-prediction price multiplied by 100,000 requests.
options.rationale: Custom model endpoints are described as provisioned capacity; no per-prediction price was read, and inventing one is the error this module warns against.

selfQuestions.prompt: The planner's query reads defect_scores WHERE production_date = yesterday and finds two rows per part after a morning rerun. Explain what the job should have written or how it should have written it so that the planner never has to guess.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Either the job overwrites the production date atomically, using replaceWhere on production_date with the date passed as a job parameter, so a rerun names yesterday and replaces its earlier rows rather than scoring today's, or it keeps both runs and the planner filters on model_version and run_id, choosing the run that the release runbook names as current. In both designs the table carries model_version, scored_at and run_id so a row's origin is explicit, and the planner's query states which version it trusts rather than taking the latest timestamp.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Provenance columns make the ambiguity visible and resolvable; an atomic overwrite is the simpler contract for a daily table, while keeping both runs preserves evidence for the release comparison. Either is acceptable if the planner's query names the version.

selfQuestions.prompt: Trace, in order, what the station's request passes through before a prediction exists, naming the identity or check at each hop, and say which two hops a malformed request never reaches and why that matters for diagnosis.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The request carries the station's service principal token to the endpoint's invocations URL; workspace authorization checks the token and the principal's permission on the endpoint; the router picks a served entity by the traffic split; the body is parsed and the signature enforced; the endpoint looks up the two features by key; the model predicts; the response returns predictions. A malformed request is refused at the signature and never reaches the lookup or the model, so a client-error spike at unchanged latency implicates the caller and not the model or the feature store.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Ordering the hops turns a status code into a location; the two unreached hops are why 4xx errors are a contract incident. Placing the router before the signature matters because each served entity enforces its own version's signature; drawing parse and enforcement as one hop is an acceptable simplification.

selfQuestions.prompt: The flagged rate falls from 9% to 3% over a morning with no release, no error and flat latency. Explain how automatic feature lookup could cause this without any request failing, and name the two scorecard rows that would have caught it earlier.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: A model logged with the feature engineering client looks up features by the keys in the request; if a key format changed, for example a supplier's lot coding, the online store holds no row, the lookup returns null, the model's imputer substitutes a value such as zero, and the score is lower for every affected part while the endpoint still answers 200. Feature freshness and key coverage, the share of requests whose lookup returned a value, are the rows that move before the flagged rate does.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The mechanism is a valid request with a wrong feature, which no status code reports; measuring lookup coverage and publish lag turns a silent skew into an alert. Monitoring the null rate on the unpacked inference table is an acceptable alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: Describe what a data profiling monitor with the InferenceLog profile needs to be told about the unpacked inference table, what two tables it writes, and why its performance metrics for this week are blank.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: It needs the timestamp column, the prediction column, a model identifier column, the problem type, the time granularity, optionally the label column and a baseline table such as the training table. It writes a profile metrics table, with per-window statistics such as count, means, null rates and the flagged rate, and a drift metrics table comparing windows to the baseline or to the previous window. Performance metrics such as precision need both a prediction column and a filled label column, and this week's rows have no labels yet because inspection results arrive one to three days later, so those windows stay blank until the join fills them.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates configuration from output and explains the blank as a property of delayed labels, not a monitor fault. Naming the metric tables' exact column names is not required, since they are read from the documentation.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the scorecard row for 'model quality' for Cinderline's endpoint as it should appear on the morning of day 20, and explain each cell.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Measure: precision on diverted parts and recall on the audit sample, stated separately. Source: inspection labels joined to the unpacked inference table, with the audit sample flagged. Owner: the model owner for the number, the quality team for the audit sample's existence. Target: precision at least 0.35, recall at least 0.6 on the audit sample. Value: not yet for day 20's windows; last verified precision 0.41 on day 17 and audit recall 0.63 over the week to day 17, 61 defective parts. Status: hypothesis until day 23, because labels arrive one to three days later and only for inspected parts. The row never shows the flagged rate as a quality value.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each cell answers one question, and the status cell carries the lag and the bias explicitly rather than hiding them in a stale number. Folding precision and recall into one accuracy figure would be a weaker answer because the two have different label sources.

beats.title: Batch and online are two contracts on one registered version
beats.outcome: Choose batch or online scoring for a consumer by who waits for the answer and how fresh its inputs must be.
beats.explanation: Cinderline's defect-risk model, version 7 under the alias champion, has two consumers. The nightly planner scores every part produced today to build tomorrow's inspection queue: nobody waits, the inputs are complete, the result is a table. The end-of-line station asks for one part's score while the part is on the belt and diverts it within 200 ms: a caller waits, the inputs exist only now, the result is a JSON response. Notice in the second state what each consumer would get from the other path. [[dbxfe-serving-batch-concept|Batch inference]] and a [[dbxfe-serving-endpoint-concept|serving endpoint]] are two contracts, not two models.

samajh.text: Socho ek dhobi hai jo poore mohalle ke kapde subah ikattha karke shaam tak dho deta hai: yeh batch hai, koi khada nahi rehta, list poori hoti hai. Aur ek istri-wala hai jo aapke saamne ek shirt turant press karta hai kyunki aapko abhi nikalna hai: yeh online hai, aap wait kar rahe ho, kaam ek-ek karke hota hai. Dono ka kaam kapde theek karna hai, par vaada alag hai: ek kehta hai shaam tak sab, doosra kehta hai abhi, sirf yeh ek.
samajh.mapping: The dhobi's evening bundle is the nightly batch job over the parts table; the istri-wala pressing one shirt while you wait is the endpoint answering one request inside its latency budget.
samajh.boundary: Behind both paths is the same registered model version, whereas the dhobi and the istri-wala are different people with different skills.

handbook.markdown:
The question that picks the path is not "how big is the data" but "who waits, and how fresh must the inputs be". A consumer that reads results later, over rows that already exist, is a batch consumer; a consumer that needs an answer for a record that exists only now, inside a latency budget, is an online consumer. Cinderline has one of each for the same registered version.

Batch inference on Databricks loads a version by name and alias, `models:/cinderline.ml.defect_risk@champion`, and applies it over a table, as a pyfunc Spark UDF or, for a model logged with feature tables, through the feature engineering client's `score_batch`; the documentation shows the alias form so that promotion changes the version scored without changing the job. Online serving is Model Serving: a managed endpoint with one URL behind which served entities run, answering `POST .../invocations` with predictions. The overview page states that Model Serving supports both real-time and batch inference for custom models, so batch can also mean calling the endpoint from SQL through `ai_query`, which the `ai_query` page says supports traditional and fully custom ML models on Model Serving endpoints. That is a third option, not a rule: it routes batch volume through the online path, and the capacity beat shows what that does to the station.

What to inspect when a team proposes one path for everything: the freshness the consumer needs, whether a caller blocks on the answer, the burst shape of the traffic, and what a failure looks like from the consumer's side. A failed batch job is a missing table and a rerun; a failed request is a part that passes uninspected. Nothing in this beat provisions anything; the choice is a design decision recorded before an endpoint exists.

beats.recap: Batch when nobody waits and the rows exist; online when a caller waits for a record that exists only now.

beats.title: A batch score is a column you write with its provenance
beats.outcome: Write a batch scoring job whose output names the version, time and run that produced every prediction.
beats.explanation: The nightly job resolves [[dbxfe-serving-batch-concept|the version by alias]], scores the day's parts with the features the model was logged with, and writes defect_risk beside model_version, scored_at and run_id. Notice in the third state why: after the alias moved to version 8 and the job reran, P-4484 has two rows, 0.41 from version 7 and 0.38 from version 8. Without the version column the planner would pick by timestamp and never know it had changed models. A scored table is evidence, and evidence names its source.

handbook.markdown:
The batch path has three parts: resolve the version, score, and write with provenance.

```python
# Nightly scoring sketch; NOT executed in this build
import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient

mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")
name = "cinderline.ml.defect_risk"
version = MlflowClient().get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion").version
run_date = dbutils.widgets.get("production_date")   # the job names the date it scores
run_id = dbutils.widgets.get("run_id")   # the job passes its run id as a parameter
parts = (spark.table("cinderline.prod.parts")
         .where(F.col("production_date") == run_date)
         .select("part_id", "production_date", "line_id", "lot_id", "oven_temp_c",
                 "belt_speed_mpm", "humidity_pct", "coat_thickness_um"))
scored = FeatureEngineeringClient().score_batch(model_uri=f"models:/{name}/{version}", df=parts)
out = (scored.select("part_id", "production_date", F.col("prediction").alias("defect_risk"))
       .withColumn("model_version", F.lit(int(version)))
       .withColumn("scored_at", F.current_timestamp())
       .withColumn("run_id", F.lit(run_id)))
(out.write.mode("overwrite")
    .option("replaceWhere", f"production_date = '{run_date}'")
    .saveAsTable("cinderline.ml.defect_scores"))
```

Resolving the alias to a number first, rather than scoring through `@champion` directly, is what lets the job write the version it used. Version 7 was logged with the feature engineering client so that the endpoint can look features up; for batch, the training-with-feature-tables page describes `score_batch`, which uses the feature metadata stored with the model to join point-in-time correct features from the offline store before scoring, with the caller supplying only the keys. A model logged with plain MLflow is scored the same way through `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf` over a frame that already holds its features. The `replaceWhere` overwrite makes a rerun replace that production date's rows atomically, provided the rerun names the date it rescores: a date taken from the clock would make the 06:40 rerun on 23 September score that morning's parts and leave the 22nd's version 7 rows in place. The third state shows the table a job that appends would leave.

Two batch alternatives exist. `ai_query` lets SQL send rows to a served model, and its page says custom ML models on Model Serving endpoints are supported; the request shape for a custom model is read from that page before use. It is convenient for small ad-hoc scoring and costly for 3,000 rows against the station's endpoint. A Spark UDF over a batch cluster or serverless job compute keeps the volume off the endpoint.

What to inspect on a scored table: the count of rows per part per day, the distribution of defect_risk against the previous run, the share above 0.35, and the version column. A change in the last one without a release note is itself a finding.

beats.recap: Resolve the alias to a version, score the day's parts, write version, time and run beside the prediction.

beats.title: An online request crosses identities before the model runs
beats.outcome: Trace one request through authorization, routing, signature enforcement, feature lookup and prediction, with a timing at each hop.
beats.explanation: The station sends its service principal's token and a body with part_id, two lookup keys and four measurements to the [[dbxfe-serving-endpoint-concept|endpoint's]] invocations URL. Authorization takes 4 ms, routing to the [[dbxfe-serving-served-entity-concept|served entity]] 1 ms, the signature check 1 ms, the feature lookup 12 ms, the model 18 ms; with 5 ms of network the round trip is 41 ms, all synthetic. Notice in the second state where a renamed column stops: at the signature, before the lookup and the model exist for that request. The third state shows what scale to zero would cost a 200 ms budget.

handbook.markdown:
Read the trace as a chain of identities. The caller is a service principal whose token the workspace validates and whose permission on the endpoint is checked; a person's token would work in a notebook but is the wrong identity for a station that runs unattended. The endpoint is one URL; behind it the router applies the traffic configuration and hands the request to a served entity, one deployed version. The body is parsed, the logged signature is enforced, then, for a model logged with the feature engineering client, the endpoint looks up features from the online store by the keys in the request, and the model predicts. The drawing is a schematic of responsibilities; the documentation does not publish a per-hop timing breakdown, and these durations are invented to show shape.

The shape is the lesson: authorization and routing are small and fixed, lookup and prediction dominate, and the total sits well inside the station's budget. Endpoint health metrics report latency over the whole path, and the metrics export API adds queue time and model latency as separate histograms, so a P99 rising from 52 ms to 400 ms without a request change can be split into queueing, lookup or model time before anyone guesses.

The second state is the incident that recurs in this module: the station app renamed a column. Schema enforcement refuses the request with a client error before any feature is read or any prediction made. The third state is why scale to zero is refused for this endpoint: the documentation says an endpoint with it enabled scales to zero after 30 minutes of inactivity, and that scaling up usually takes ten to twenty seconds, sometimes minutes, with no SLA.

```python
# Station-side call sketch; NOT executed in this build
import requests
body = {"dataframe_split": {
    "columns": ["part_id", "line_id", "lot_id", "oven_temp_c", "belt_speed_mpm", "humidity_pct", "coat_thickness_um"],
    "data": [["P-4471", "L3", "K-22", 212.5, 3.2, 61.0, 48.7]]}}
r = requests.post(f"{host}/serving-endpoints/defect-risk/invocations",
                  headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, json=body, timeout=0.2)
```

`timeout=0.2` bounds the connection and each socket read, not the whole call, so a hard 200 ms deadline needs the station's own timer or a client with a total timeout. Past it, the request is abandoned and Cinderline's station fails open: the part continues uninspected. That is a design choice whose cost is missed defects; failing closed would send it to the inspection lane and cost lane capacity instead.

beats.recap: Token, endpoint, served entity, signature, lookup, model: a refusal stops at the signature and a cold start stops the clock.

beats.title: The request contract is the signature made external
beats.outcome: Predict, for a given request body, whether the server accepts it, casts it or refuses it, and at which layer.
beats.explanation: The body is a JSON-serialized pandas DataFrame under dataframe_split or dataframe_records, and two layers act on it. Parsing casts values to the signature's types, so 61 or "61" becomes 61.0, while "61%" cannot be cast and is refused. Then [[dbxfe-serving-signature-concept|enforcement]] matches columns by name, refuses a missing required column, ignores an undeclared one and allows only lossless conversions. Notice in the second state that a renamed column is a missing required column, and in the fourth why the [[dbxfe-serving-contract-concept|contract]] test sends JSON.
beats.hint: Ask four questions of each column: is it declared, is it present, can the parser cast it, and is the result lossless.

handbook.markdown:
The MLflow signature guide states the enforcement rules. Enforcement runs when a model is loaded as a python function or served through deployment tools; it does not run for a model loaded in its native flavor, so a notebook that calls `mlflow.sklearn.load_model` may predict on a renamed frame the endpoint refuses. Inputs are matched by name and reordered to the signature's order; missing required inputs raise; extra inputs are disregarded; for column-based signatures only lossless conversions pass, int to double but not long to double.

Before enforcement, the server parses the body. Open-source MLflow's scoring server accepts exactly one of `dataframe_split`, `dataframe_records`, `instances` or `inputs`, and passes the signature to its JSON parser, which casts values to the signature's types; a value it cannot cast is refused as a bad request. The Databricks SDK for Python's API reference for the query call lists the same four input fields for DataFrame and tensor input, posted to the endpoint's `/serving-endpoints/{name}/invocations` path, with `predictions` in the response. Whether the managed endpoint's parser casts exactly as the open-source one does is a verification item, checked at stage 1 of a release by its 4xx rate, not assumed.

Two consequences follow. A test that builds a pandas frame from Python integers holds int64, MLflow's long, and is refused where the JSON path would accept the same number; test the body, not a frame. And a null in a declared column is not a missing column: it passes both layers and reaches the model as a missing value, which is why the scorecard counts nulls.

The lesson's contract test therefore rebuilds the version's signature around a constant stand-in model and sends JSON bodies through the open-source handler: the column list, a valid body, a missing column, a renamed column and a unit suffix. It is labelled not executed in this build, calls no endpoint, and proves the contract, not the model's predictions. A signature changes only with a new version, so a caller's schema change is a caller fix or a new release.

beats.recap: Parse casts to the signature's types, enforcement checks names and lossless types; test the JSON body, not a frame.
beats.changeNote: The handbook now credits the request's four DataFrame and tensor input fields, its invocations path and its predictions response field to the Databricks SDK for Python's API reference (v0.141.0, read on 2026-09-25) instead of the query documentation page. What the beat teaches is unchanged.

beats.title: Concurrency is a count in flight and latency is what the queue adds
beats.outcome: Estimate whether an endpoint's provisioned concurrency carries a caller without queueing, and say what scale to zero costs a latency budget.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-serving-concurrency-concept|Provisioned concurrency]] is a count of requests in flight, not a speed: the load a caller offers is its arrival rate times service time. The station, about 0.05 requests per second over two shifts at 41 ms, offers 0.002 against a Small endpoint's four units. Notice the third state: the planner's 3,000 parts at 60 per second with 80 ms service offer 4.8 to four units, so the backlog grows every second of the burst and the station waits seconds. [[dbxfe-serving-scale-zero-concept|Scale to zero]] lowers the floor to zero after idleness and charges a cold start.

samajh.text: Bank mein chaar counter khule hain. Har customer ko lagbhag ek minute lagta hai. Agar har minute do log aate hain, counters khaali rehte hain. Agar shift ke shuru mein har minute paanch log aane lagein, toh har minute ek aadmi line mein judta jaata hai: counter tez nahi hue, bas queue lambi hoti ja rahi hai. Aur agar bank ne raat ko counters band kar diye, toh subah pehla customer taala khulne ka intezaar karega, chahe woh akela hi kyun na ho.
samajh.mapping: Counters are provisioned concurrency, minutes per customer are the model's service time, the growing line is the backlog that becomes added latency, and the locked door at morning is a cold start after scale to zero.
samajh.boundary: A larger endpoint adds counters automatically within its workload size range, and its locked door opens in seconds to minutes with no promised time, unlike a bank's fixed opening hour.

handbook.markdown:
The documentation maps each workload size to a range of provisioned concurrency, Small 4, Medium 8 to 16 and Large 16 to 64 as read at search time, states that one unit processes one request at a time, and estimates the concurrency a workload needs as queries per second multiplied by model execution time. That is the relation this beat uses. Four units at 80 ms each serve 50 requests per second; 60 arriving per second leaves 10 per second unserved, so over the planner's 50-second burst a backlog of about 500 builds and the last arrival waits about ten seconds. A Small endpoint's range is four to four, so autoscaling does not rescue it; a larger size autoscales within its range, and scale-up is not instant. In this schematic the excess waits; how the endpoint signals load beyond its limits, delay or refusal, is read from the current limits and debugging pages. Either way the station loses. Averages understate bursts; size for the peak minute, not the day.

Three consequences for Cinderline. First, keep the planner off the endpoint: batch scoring on job compute handles 3,000 parts without touching the station's path. Second, if a second online caller must share the endpoint, raise the workload size or give it its own endpoint; both are cost decisions the cost beat lists as drivers, not numbers. Third, scale to zero is refused for defect-risk: the documentation says it scales an endpoint down after 30 minutes of inactivity, that scaling up usually takes ten to twenty seconds and sometimes minutes with no SLA, and that it is not for workloads needing guaranteed response times. It suits an internal tool whose user can wait.

What to inspect when latency rises: queue time and model latency from the exported metrics, request rate, CPU and memory; the inference table for a new requester or a larger request; the lookup path for online store latency. Rising queue time with flat model latency is capacity; rising model latency is the model or its lookup.

beats.recap: Offered load is rate times service time; past the units the backlog is your latency, and a cold start is a queue with no clock.

beats.title: Features at inference are looked up, not sent
beats.outcome: Explain what a request carries when a model uses automatic feature lookup and what a missing or stale key produces.
beats.explanation: The station cannot compute the line's defect rate over the last eight hours, so the request carries only keys and on-belt measurements and the endpoint performs an [[dbxfe-serving-lookup-concept|automatic feature lookup]] from an online store by line_id and lot_id. Notice in the second state what a supplier's lot-coding change does: the key is in no row, the lookup returns null, the model imputes zero, the score falls from 0.42 to 0.11 and the response is 200. Nothing failed; the contract was met and the answer was wrong, because zero-imputing a missing lookup breaks the features module's missingness policy.

handbook.markdown:
The automatic feature lookup page states that, for a model logged with the feature engineering client's `log_model`, Model Serving uses the keys in the request to retrieve the published feature values the model needs from an online store, a Databricks Online Feature Store, which the online store page describes as powered by Lakebase, or a supported third-party store. Features reach that store by publishing a Unity Catalog feature table to it. The training side, point-in-time joins so that training rows see only features available at production time, is the features module's; this beat is its serving half, and consistency between the two is the reason to log the model with its feature specification rather than have callers assemble features themselves.

The failure modes are silent. A stale store, because the publishing job is late, serves yesterday's line rate with a 200 response. A missing key, after a coding change on the caller's side or in the feature pipeline, serves nulls, and Cinderline's model, trained to impute a missing value as zero, turns them into a plausible number. In Cinderline's day-20 incident the supplier's lot coding changed, `supplier_lot_reject_rate_30d` became null for every part from that supplier, the imputed zero read as a clean supplier, the flagged rate fell to 3%, and inspection of the parts recalled after the backfill later verified defects that had passed uninspected. The pipeline fix and a backfill repaired the day, but the design defect was the zero imputation, which the features module's missingness policy rules out: zero is a measurement. A lookup miss should come back as an explicit no-score that the station handles by a rule the owner writes, for example diverting the part at the inspection lane's cost, not as a 200 with an invented value.

Put two rows on the scorecard for this: feature freshness, here the time since the latest publish (publish lag, not the features module's value age), and lookup coverage, the share of requests whose lookup found a row. Both are readable before any label arrives. Unpacking the inference table and counting nulls per feature is the cheapest version.

beats.recap: Keys in, features from the store; a missing key is a 200 with a wrong answer, so measure freshness and coverage.

beats.title: A release is a traffic split you can read and reverse
beats.outcome: Plan a staged release as traffic percentages with an evidence gate per stage and a one-step rollback that keeps the previous entity.
beats.explanation: Version 8 joins the endpoint as a second served entity at 10% [[dbxfe-serving-traffic-concept|traffic]]. Both run; the inference table records which entity answered each request, so the two are compared over the same windows: errors, P99, flagged rate. Gates pass, 50%, then 100% with version 7 kept deployed for seven days. Notice the second state: 5xx on version 8 alone, and three minutes later one configuration update makes version 7 100%. That [[dbxfe-serving-rollback-concept|rollback]] needs the old entity to still exist.

samajh.text: Naye halwai ko dukaan par rakhne se pehle purana halwai poora din nahi hataya jaata. Pehle naya sirf dus mein se ek order banata hai, purana baaki nau. Grahakon ki raay aur wapas aaye plates dekhe jaate hain, phir aadha-aadha, phir poora. Agar shikayat aaye, toh order wapas purane ko de do. Naya halwai abhi bhi dukaan mein hai, bas order nahi le raha, aur uski galti aaram se dekhi ja sakti hai.
samajh.mapping: The two halwais are two served entities on one endpoint, the share of orders is the traffic split, and handing orders back to the old halwai is a rollback by traffic rather than a redeploy.
samajh.boundary: Real customers can see which halwai cooked; the endpoint's callers see one URL and cannot choose a served entity, which is why the inference table must record who answered.

handbook.markdown:
The serve-multiple-models page states that one endpoint can serve several models or versions, each a served entity with a traffic percentage, that the split is part of the endpoint configuration and changed by updating it, and that an endpoint can have at most ten served entities. The endpoint page shows the shape: `served_entities` naming the registered model and version with a workload size and scale-to-zero flag, and `traffic_config` with routes carrying `traffic_percentage` for each served entity by name.

```json
{"served_entities": [
   {"name": "defect_risk-7", "entity_name": "cinderline.ml.defect_risk", "entity_version": "7", "workload_size": "Small", "scale_to_zero_enabled": false},
   {"name": "defect_risk-8", "entity_name": "cinderline.ml.defect_risk", "entity_version": "8", "workload_size": "Small", "scale_to_zero_enabled": false}],
 "traffic_config": {"routes": [
   {"served_entity_name": "defect_risk-7", "traffic_percentage": 90},
   {"served_entity_name": "defect_risk-8", "traffic_percentage": 10}]}}
```

This configuration is illustrative and not applied in this build. A staged release is a sequence of such updates with a gate before each: stage 0 is the local contract test and a batch replay of last week's logged requests through version 8, compared with version 7's logged responses; stage 1 is 10% for two days, gated on error rate, P99 inside the budget and the flagged rate within its band, all read per served entity from the inference table; stage 2 is 50%, adding precision on diverted parts once labels arrive for the canary windows; stage 3 is 100% with version 7 retained.

Rollback is the same lever in reverse: version 7 to 100%, version 8 to 0%, kept deployed so its service logs can be read while it serves nothing. Read the endpoint's state after the update and declare the rollback done only when the new configuration is reported live. Deleting the old entity on promotion, or deleting the endpoint, converts a three-minute reversal into a redeploy with a build and a startup while the station fails. The alias in the registry moves separately; a rollback by traffic does not move it, so the release runbook says which of the two is the source of truth for batch, which loads by alias.

beats.recap: Add the new entity, earn traffic by gates, keep the old entity, and roll back by moving traffic, never by deleting.

beats.title: Inference tables make every request a row you can join
beats.outcome: Turn logged requests into a labelled evidence table and say which rows will never receive a label.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-serving-inference-table-concept|inference table]] writes each request as a Delta row: time, status code, the served entity, execution time, the request and response bodies. Notice the 06:10 rows in the first state: status 400 from both entities, the renamed column in the body, five milliseconds each, the contract incident recorded as data. Unpack the bodies and every prediction sits beside its inputs and its entity. Join inspection results by part_id three days later and some rows gain a label. P-4489 was never inspected; its label stays null.

handbook.markdown:
The inference tables page states that the endpoint automatically captures incoming requests and outgoing responses and logs them as a Unity Catalog Delta table, and that joining it with ground-truth labels builds a training and evaluation corpus. Two variants are documented, the AI Gateway-enabled tables that Databricks recommends and a legacy variant, with different column names and prerequisites; read the page that applies to the endpoint before writing a query, and expect columns for request time, status code, the served entity, execution time and the request and response payloads. Logging is not instant: the table is created after the first request, and rows can take up to an hour to appear, so the inference table is evidence for analysis and the endpoint's health metrics remain the first alarm.

Unpacking is a query, sketched here and not executed:

```sql
-- Unpacking sketch; NOT executed in this build. The column names below are placeholders:
-- replace them with the names on the inference-table page that applies to the endpoint.
SELECT request_time, served_entity, status_code,
       from_json(request, 'STRUCT<dataframe_split: STRUCT<columns: ARRAY<STRING>, data: ARRAY<ARRAY<STRING>>>>') AS req,
       from_json(response, 'STRUCT<predictions: ARRAY<DOUBLE>>').predictions[0] AS defect_risk
FROM cinderline.ml.defect_risk_inference
WHERE status_code = 200;
```

The unpacked table is the input to everything downstream: the canary comparison per served entity over identical windows, the null-rate count per feature that catches a lookup failure, the data profiling monitor, and the label join. Labels arrive with a lag and for a biased subset: diverted parts are inspected because the model flagged them, the 5% audit sample is inspected regardless, and everything else is labelled only by a customer return, weeks later or never. A join therefore produces three kinds of rows, labelled by inspection, labelled by return, and unlabelled, and any quality number states which kind it used.

What to inspect: the share of 4xx and 5xx by hour and by requester, execution time percentiles per entity, payload sizes, and the count of rows per part_id per day, which should be one.

beats.recap: Every request becomes a row with its entity and bodies; unpack it, join labels later, and say which rows stay unlabelled.

beats.title: A monitor profiles windows and compares them to a baseline
beats.outcome: Read a data profiling monitor's profile and drift tables and say when its performance metrics can exist.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-serving-profiling-concept|data profiling monitor]], formerly Lakehouse Monitoring, with the InferenceLog profile summarizes the unpacked inference table by time window: counts, means, null rates, the flagged rate. Against a baseline, the training table, it writes drift metrics per column. Notice in the second state what moved on day 20 at 08:00: the supplier feature's null rate and the prediction mean, not humidity. In the third state, precision and recall exist only for windows whose label column is filled; this week's are blank, and that blank is honest.

handbook.markdown:
The data profiling page states that the feature was formerly known as Lakehouse Monitoring, that it profiles Delta tables in Unity Catalog, computes quality metrics, detects drift and produces dashboards, and that it has three profile types, time series, snapshot and inference; for an inference profile it also computes model performance and drift metrics, and a good baseline is the data used to train or validate the model. The metric tables page states that a monitor writes a profile metrics table and a drift metrics table, that the drift table exists only when a baseline is given or consecutive windows exist, and that InferenceLog performance metrics need both a prediction column and a label column, with extra metrics for classification. Data profiling belongs to the data quality monitoring family, which the documentation says runs on serverless compute under its own billing product and does not modify the tables it monitors; the page for the older `quality_monitors` API is marked deprecated, so a monitor scripted from an old notebook is checked against the current page before it is reused.

A monitor therefore answers questions about windows: what did an hour of requests look like, and how does it differ from training data or from the previous hour. It does not answer questions about a request; the inference table does that. For Cinderline the monitor sits on the unpacked table with hourly granularity, the training table as baseline, `defect_risk` as prediction, `label` as the label column that the inspection join fills later, and the served entity as the model identifier so that a canary's two versions profile separately.

Read the tables in this order: null rates and counts first, because a lookup failure or a caller change shows there before anything else; then drift per input column; then prediction drift; then performance for the windows that have labels. The day-20 signature is unmistakable in that order: in the 08:00 window the supplier feature's null rate jumps to 38% and the flagged rate falls to 3%, while humidity stays inside its baseline. What the monitor cannot say is whether the lower scores were wrong; that waits for labels, which the next beat takes up.

beats.recap: Profile per window, drift against a baseline, performance only where labels exist; read nulls first.

beats.title: Drift is a hypothesis until delayed labels test it
beats.outcome: Mark each event on a monitoring timeline as known or hypothesized and say which labels would settle the hypothesis.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-serving-drift-concept|Drift]] is measured the day it happens: humidity outside its baseline on day 1, the flagged rate at 16% on day 2. 'The model is worse' is a hypothesis. [[dbxfe-serving-delayed-label-concept|Delayed labels]] arrive from day 4: precision on diverted parts 0.41 against 0.40, audit recall unchanged, hypothesis refuted; defects really rose. Notice the second state: on day 20 the same hypothesis is confirmed by labels on the recalled parts, 12 defective parts that had passed, and the cause is a feature pipeline, so the fix is the pipeline and a backfill, not a retrain.

samajh.text: Ek doctor ke paas ek hafte mein bukhaar ke mareez double ho gaye. Pehli soch: kya thermometer kharab hai? Yeh sirf shak hai. Jab tak lab reports nahi aatin, pata nahi chalta ki thermometer galat hai ya sach mein bukhaar phail raha hai. Reports teen din baad aayi: bukhaar sach mein tha. Thermometer theek tha, mausam badla tha. Agli baar agar reports kahein ki bukhaar nahi tha, tab thermometer par shak pakka hoga.
samajh.mapping: The doubled fever count is prediction drift, the thermometer is the model, the lab reports are delayed labels, and the changed weather is a real shift in the parts arriving.
samajh.boundary: Labels here arrive only for inspected parts, so unlike lab reports they cover a biased sample unless an audit sample is inspected regardless of the score.

handbook.markdown:
Two words keep this honest. Known means a measurement exists: a drift statistic, a null rate, a flagged rate, a status code. Hypothesized means an inference from measurements to something not yet measured, usually "the model's predictions are now worse". The gap between them is the label lag: Cinderline's inspection results arrive one to three days after a part is scored, for diverted parts and for a random 5% audit sample, and a part that passed uninspected is labelled only if a customer returns it.

Selection bias follows from that. Precision on diverted parts is measurable with a lag because those parts were inspected. Recall needs labels on parts the model did not flag, which only the audit sample provides: 150 parts a day, of which about nine are defective, so recall is estimated over a trailing week, about 60 defective parts, and reported with that count. On day 20 the affected parts could be named, because their feature was null, so the backfill rescored them and inspection of the recalled ones settled the question faster than the audit sample could have; a silent recall loss that names no parts leaves only the audit sample. Without the audit sample, a model that stopped flagging defective parts would look better every week: fewer diversions, the same precision, and no labels on the parts it missed. The audit sample is the single most important operational decision in this module, and it belongs to the quality team, not the model.

The two episodes end differently. In the humid season the inputs moved because the world moved; the model tracked it; the operational problem was inspection capacity, which the planner needed to know on day 2, not day 5. In the supplier episode the inputs moved because a pipeline broke; the model's scores were wrong; the fix was in the pipeline and the zero imputation that hid the miss, a backfill of the feature values for the affected windows, and a batch rescoring of those parts so the planner could recall the ones now above 0.35; retraining on those windows would have taught the model that null means clean.

Pre-declare expected shifts, the humid season, a new supplier, a line rebuild, so that a drift alert alone does not open a quality incident. Record on the timeline what was known at each time, so a later reader sees the decision as it was made.

beats.recap: Measured is known; 'worse' is a hypothesis; labels arrive late and only for some rows, so keep an audit sample.

beats.title: Classify the incident by the layer that produced its evidence
beats.outcome: Route an alert to one of four incident classes and name its first check and mitigation.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-serving-incident-concept|incident]] is named by its evidence. Endpoint health: 5xx, timeouts, latency with no request change. Contract: a 4xx spike after a caller change. Data and features: nulls, freshness, drift. Verified quality loss: labelled windows worse than baseline. Notice in the second state that day 12's renamed column never touches the health or quality classes, and that a rollback would have changed nothing because both entities enforce the same signature. Rollback by traffic answers the first class and, when a release preceded the loss, the last.

handbook.markdown:
The monitoring page names the evidence each class reads: endpoint health metrics for latency, request rate, error rate, CPU and memory; service logs for a container's stdout and stderr; build logs for the environment build; and data profiling for performance and drift. The debugging guide is the documented first stop when a deployment fails to build or start. The inference table adds per-request status codes and bodies, and labels add verified quality.

Endpoint health. Evidence: 5xx, timeouts, P99 rising with flat request bodies. First check: per-entity health metrics, then service logs of the failing entity. Mitigation: if a release is in progress, traffic to the previous entity; otherwise capacity, a dependency in the lookup path, or a container fault that the logs name.

Contract. Evidence: a 4xx spike, usually at flat latency because refused requests are cheap. First check: the 4xx count in the endpoint metrics and the caller's deployment log, then the inference table's request bodies against the signature once they land, up to an hour later. Mitigation: revert the caller or map the field on the caller's side. Never widen the signature under incident; a wider signature is a new version that re-enters the release stages.

Data and features. Evidence: null rates, publish lag, drift in inputs or predictions. First check: lookup coverage and freshness, then the pipeline's last successful run. Mitigation: fix the pipeline, backfill the affected windows, hold any rollout, replace any zero imputation of a missing lookup with an explicit no-score, and record the quality question as a hypothesis.

Verified quality loss. Evidence: labelled windows worse than baseline, precision on diverted parts or recall on the audit sample. First check: which windows, which served entity, and whether a release or a data incident preceded them. Mitigation: traffic rollback if a release caused it; a pipeline fix if data caused it; retraining only when the world changed and the labels say the old decision boundary no longer holds.

Every incident closes into a record of what was known at each time and what was hypothesized, so the runbook improves and the scorecard's thresholds are argued from cases rather than guesses.

beats.recap: Name the class by its evidence: health, contract, data, or verified quality; only two of the four are answered by rollback.

beats.title: A scorecard names the measurement, its source and its owner
beats.outcome: Fill an operational scorecard in which every row has a source, an owner, a target and a known or hypothesized status.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-serving-scorecard-concept|operational scorecard]] is a table, not a dashboard: measure, source, owner, target, value, status. The source column is the discipline: endpoint metrics for availability and P99, the inference table for status codes, the online store's publish time for freshness, the unpacked table for lookup coverage, the monitor for the flagged rate, labels with their lag for precision, billing for cost. Notice in the second state which rows change on day 20 and which say hypothesis: coverage and the flagged rate are known breaches, quality is not yet measurable.

handbook.markdown:
A scorecard row is a small contract. The measure says what is counted and over which window. The source says which system can actually produce the number, which stops a team from reporting a feeling as a metric: availability, P99 and the 4xx and 5xx counts come from endpoint health metrics, which the metrics export API can deliver to Prometheus or Datadog, while the inference table's status codes and bodies, which can arrive up to an hour later, explain them; feature freshness from the publish time of the online store, meaning publish lag, not the features module's value age; lookup coverage from the null rate on the unpacked table; the flagged rate and input drift from the data profiling monitor; precision from inspection labels with their lag and recall from the audit sample over a week, with its count of defective parts; cost from billing once a pricing page has been read. The owner is the team that can move the number, which for a 4xx rate is the station app's team, not the model owner. The target is argued from cases, the 200 ms budget for latency, the 6 to 12% band for the flagged rate, and stated as a trigger rather than a verdict where the measure is a drift.

The status column carries the epistemics: known, known with a lag, hypothesis, unmeasurable until labels arrive, or unknown until pricing is checked. On a normal day it is dull, which is the point; on day 20 it shows coverage and the flagged rate as known breaches and quality as a hypothesis with a date attached. Recall is reported over a trailing week because a day's audit sample holds about nine defective parts, too few for a daily number.

What a scorecard omits on purpose: an overall health score that averages rows with different owners; any number without a source; a cost figure without a dated pricing source; and a quality number that silently uses only diverted parts. Review it weekly with the label join, and after every incident add or retire a row based on what the incident needed and did not have.

beats.recap: Measure, source, owner, target, value, status: a row without a source is a feeling, a drift without labels is a hypothesis.

beats.title: Cost follows provisioned hours and stored rows, not predictions alone
beats.outcome: Name the cost drivers of the online and batch paths and say what each design change moves on the bill and on the scorecard.
beats.explanation: The online path holds provisioned capacity for every hour of the month, 720 at the Small size, including the idle third shift, plus the inference table's rows, the monitor's refreshes and the online store's hours. The batch path pays for its minutes and nothing between runs. Notice the third state: every [[dbxfe-serving-cost-concept|cost driver]] you cut moves a row on the scorecard, scale to zero moves P99 on the first morning request, and shorter retention moves the label join. Rates stay symbols until a pricing page is read.

handbook.markdown:
This beat prices nothing. The documentation describes custom model endpoints as provisioned capacity in workload sizes, with scale to zero as the option that releases it when idle; inference tables as Delta tables that grow with requests; and data quality monitoring as serverless compute billed under its own billing product. Those are the drivers. Their rates, and the exact billing unit for serving, come from the current pricing page for the cloud, region and edition in use, with a date attached.

Online drivers, for Cinderline: provisioned hours, 24 × 30 at Small, eight of each 24 idle between shifts, moved by workload size and by scale to zero, which is refused because of the cold start; inference-table storage, about 90,000 rows a month at 3,000 parts a day, small here and large on a busier endpoint, moved by retention and by request sampling; monitor refreshes, moved by granularity and schedule; and the online store's instance hours and any read replicas. Batch drivers: job compute minutes, 30 runs of 12 minutes on a small cluster or serverless job compute, doubled on a day with a rerun; storage for the scored table; nothing between runs.

The useful exercise is the third state, a change and its two consequences. Scale to zero cuts idle hours and breaches P99 every morning. A Medium size costs more and buys headroom for a second caller. Cutting inference-table retention from 90 to 14 days cuts storage and means a label that arrives on day 15 joins nothing, which for customer-return labels is most of them. Moving the monitor from hourly to daily cuts refreshes and delays the day-20 signature by hours. Each saving is legitimate; each is recorded beside the scorecard row it moves, and the operations lead chooses.

Write the cost row of the scorecard as unknown with its drivers listed until pricing is checked; a number without a dated source is a guess wearing a currency symbol.

beats.recap: Hours provisioned, rows kept, refreshes run: cut any of them and name the scorecard row that moves; price nothing without a dated page.

extensionCards.prompt: When would Cinderline evaluate a route-optimized endpoint for the station?
extensionCards.answer: When overhead latency, not model time, threatens the budget; route optimization is chosen when an endpoint is created and is queried at its own URL with OAuth tokens.
extensionCards.explanation: The request trace shows fixed overheads before the model runs. If the station's budget tightened to 50 ms, those overheads would matter as much as the 18 ms of prediction. The documentation describes [[dbxfe-serving-extension-route-optimization-concept|route optimization]] as a shorter network path that lowers overhead latency and supports higher queries per second. Two operational facts decide the plan: the setting is specified when an endpoint is created and cannot be added to an existing one, so adopting it means a new endpoint and a caller switch, staged like any release; and a route-optimized endpoint is queried at a different URL with OAuth tokens, not personal access tokens, so the station's service principal needs an OAuth flow. Supported endpoint types and availability are read from the current page; the timing estimate is repeated after the switch.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Names the documented option for the overhead half of latency and keeps it a verification item.

extensionCards.prompt: How does the endpoint's P99 reach the plant's existing Prometheus dashboard?
extensionCards.answer: Through the documented metrics export API, which exposes endpoint health metrics in OpenMetrics form for Prometheus or Datadog to scrape.
extensionCards.explanation: The monitoring page says endpoint health metrics cover latency, request rate, error rate, CPU and memory. The [[dbxfe-serving-extension-metrics-export-concept|metrics export]] page shows how an API delivers them to Prometheus and Datadog, including request latency, model latency and queue time as histograms and 4xx and 5xx counts; reading it needs read access to the endpoint and an access token. A P99 is computed from the latency histogram, and the queue-time histogram separates capacity from model time. For Cinderline this puts the endpoint rows on the same board as the line's own sensors. Metric names and scrape intervals are read from the current page.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Gives the scorecard's endpoint rows an exportable source outside the workspace UI.

extensionCards.prompt: Version 8 fails to reach a ready state on the endpoint. Where do you read first?
extensionCards.answer: The build log for the environment build, then the service log for the container's stdout and stderr, with the debugging guide as the documented list of common causes.
extensionCards.explanation: A served entity is built into a Python environment before it serves; a missing pin, a conflicting dependency or a model that cannot load fails there, before any request exists. The monitoring page names [[dbxfe-serving-extension-build-logs-concept|build logs]] for the environment build and service logs for the container's stdout and stderr, and the debugging guide collects common failures around builds, dependencies and startup. In the release runbook this fails before stage 1 takes any traffic: nothing was routed, nothing rolled back, and the fix is a new version logged with a corrected environment, which the MLflow module's environment beat covers.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Separates a deployment that never started from an incident on a serving entity.

extensionCards.prompt: Can a SQL analyst score a small table of returned parts against the served model without Python?
extensionCards.answer: Yes, where documented: ai_query sends rows to a served model from SQL and supports traditional and custom ML models on Model Serving endpoints.
extensionCards.explanation: The ai_query page states that it queries served models from SQL or Python and supports traditional ML models, including fully custom ones, when deployed on Model Serving endpoints. For a few hundred returned parts that is convenient and keeps provenance in one query. Two cautions follow from this module: the request shape for a custom model is read from the function page, and the rows travel through the online endpoint, so a large [[dbxfe-serving-extension-ai-query-concept|ai_query]] scan competes with the station for provisioned concurrency; the capacity beat's estimate applies before running it during a shift.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Names the SQL route to a served model and ties it to the capacity estimate.

recap.title: One version, two contracts, evidence before verdicts
recap.markdown: **Batch and online are two contracts on one registered version:** a scored table with its provenance, and an endpoint that answers one request inside a budget. The request crosses a token, a served entity, the signature, a feature lookup and the model, and it stops at the signature when the contract breaks. Concurrency is a count in flight; scale to zero charges a cold start. A release is a traffic split with a gate per stage and a rollback that keeps the old entity. The inference table makes every request a row, the monitor summarizes windows against a baseline, and drift stays a hypothesis until delayed labels, biased toward diverted parts unless an audit sample exists, test it. An incident is classified by the layer that produced its evidence, the scorecard names a source and an owner for every row, and cost is drivers until a pricing page is read. **Transfer challenge:** redraw the request trace, the scorecard and the release stages for a warranty-claim fraud model whose labels arrive after 90 days and whose caller is a claims web form with a two-second budget; mark what scale to zero would now be allowed to do.

appliedTask.title: Release version 8 to the second plant
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline's second plant gets its own defect-risk endpoint. Its station has a 500 ms budget, its inspection labels arrive after seven days, it runs one shift, and the humid season is already under way there. Write the contract test cases you would add or change, the scorecard rows whose target or status differs from the first plant, and the staged release with its gates and rollback, saying which gate cannot close until labels arrive and what scale to zero would now cost.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Contract test: the same five cases against the version's signature, plus a case for the second plant's station payload if any column name or unit format differs, run locally and never against the endpoint. Scorecard: P99 target 300 ms under a 500 ms budget rather than 120; precision on diverted parts marked hypothesis for seven days rather than three, with the row stating the lag; flagged-rate band re-derived from this plant's baseline because the humid season is already in the data, and the season pre-declared as an expected shift so a drift alert alone opens no quality incident; lookup coverage and freshness unchanged; cost unknown until pricing is checked, with one-shift hours listed as the driver. Release: stage 0 contract test and a batch replay of the second plant's last two weeks of logged requests; stage 1 at 10% for three days, gated on error rate, P99 and flagged rate per served entity from the inference table; stage 2 at 50%, whose precision gate cannot close until day 7 labels arrive, so the stage lasts at least a week; stage 3 at 100% with the previous entity retained for fourteen days because rollback evidence takes longer to arrive. Rollback is one traffic change. Scale to zero: with one shift and a 500 ms budget it is still refused, because the cold start is seconds to minutes, not hundreds of milliseconds; it would save the sixteen idle hours a day and breach P99 on the first request of every morning.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer re-derives targets from the new budget and label lag instead of copying them, keeps the quality gate honest about when labels exist, and prices scale to zero as a scorecard consequence rather than a saving.
